description: Practical constraints of time, cost and access. Ethical issues of consent, confidentiality and harm.
content_html:
Why Practical and Ethical Issues Matter

Even the most theoretically sophisticated research design is worthless if it cannot be put into practice or if it causes harm to the people involved. The AQA specification requires students to understand two distinct categories of constraints on sociological research: practical issues (the real-world limitations of time, cost and access) and ethical issues (the moral obligations researchers owe to participants and to society). Crucially, the spec asks not only that students identify these issues but that they explain how researchers address them.

Practical Issues: Time, Cost and Access

Time is a fundamental constraint. A longitudinal study tracking a cohort of children from birth to adulthood might take decades to produce findings — valuable, but beyond the resources of most researchers. A PhD student conducting a dissertation study has months, not years. The method must match the available timescale: participant observation is time-intensive; a self-completion questionnaire distributed via email is not.

Cost constrains the scale and type of research. A large-scale national survey with a team of interviewers and a random sample of 5,000 households requires substantial funding. Academic sociologists apply to research councils; independent researchers may be limited to small local studies. Online questionnaires have dramatically reduced the cost of reaching large samples, but interviewer-led or observational methods remain expensive in labour time.

Access is often the decisive practical constraint. Some groups are hard to reach: gang members, people experiencing domestic abuse, children in care, undocumented migrants. Gatekeepers — head teachers, prison governors, social workers, community leaders — must often be persuaded before the researcher can reach participants at all. Gatekeepers can improve access but can also limit it: a head teacher who restricts research to “well-behaved” pupils introduces sampling bias by excluding the most relevant participants for a study of school exclusion.

Key Fact

The three practical issues are time, cost and access. All three affect which method is feasible and whether the resulting sample will be representative. Access is often the most sociologically interesting: the hardest populations to reach are frequently those whose experiences are most poorly understood and most important to study.

Ethical Issues: Consent, Confidentiality and Harm

The British Sociological Association (BSA) publishes ethical guidelines that professional sociologists are expected to follow. At GCSE level, three ethical issues are named in the specification: informed consent, confidentiality and harm to participants.

Informed consent means participants must be told — in plain language — what the study is about, how their data will be used, and that they can withdraw at any time without penalty. The “informed” element is crucial: obtaining permission for a vaguely described study is not genuine consent. The “voluntary” element is also critical: participants in a prison, a school or a workplace may feel unable to refuse without consequences, even if they are technically told they can.

Confidentiality means that identifying information about participants must be protected. In practice, this means anonymising names and locations in published findings, storing data securely, and not sharing raw data in ways that allow individuals to be identified. Even where participants have consented to take part, they have a right to expect that personal details will not be disclosed to employers, family members or the authorities.

Harm to participants covers a wide range of potential risks: psychological distress from discussing traumatic experiences, physical risk from studying dangerous settings, reputational damage from being identified in publications, or criminal liability from disclosing involvement in illegal activities. The researcher has a duty to anticipate and minimise these risks, not simply to note that they exist.

The spec explicitly asks how ethical issues can be addressed. Students should know practical solutions, not just list the problems:

  • Informed consent: use a written consent form in plain English; for children, obtain parental consent as well; include a clear explanation of withdrawal rights at the start of every session.
  • Confidentiality: anonymise all names and locations in transcripts and publications; use participant codes rather than names in data files; store data on password-protected systems; delete raw recordings after transcription.
  • Harm: offer a debrief session after the research, particularly if sensitive topics were discussed; provide signposting to support services (e.g. domestic abuse helplines); have a clear protocol for stopping the research if a participant shows signs of distress; obtain ethics committee approval before beginning.
  • Deception: covert research necessarily involves deception, which violates the BSA’s informed consent principle. Researchers must justify covert methods by arguing that the social benefit of the knowledge justifies the ethical cost, and must debrief participants as soon as possible after completion.

The Tension Between Research Goals and Ethics

Ethical requirements can directly conflict with research goals. Informed consent can alter participants’ behaviour (if people know they are being studied, they may act differently — the Hawthorne effect). Confidentiality limits what researchers can report. Harm avoidance may prevent researchers from accessing the most important settings. A sociologist wanting to study violence within prison gangs faces an almost irresolvable tension: the most valid data would come from covert observation or candid interviews, but gaining access covertly is deceptive and putting researchers in a violent environment raises serious safety concerns.

Different sociological perspectives can also generate different ethical pressures. A feminist researcher studying violence against women may feel ethically obliged to empower participants rather than simply extract data from them — an approach sometimes called participatory research, in which participants are involved in shaping the research process. A positivist researcher, by contrast, may prioritise objectivity and distance, arguing that participant involvement would compromise validity.

A persistent exam error is to list “consent, confidentiality, harm” as three boxes to tick without reasoning about which apply to the specific research scenario and how the researcher addresses them. For a study of attitudes to unemployment benefit, harm is a relatively minor concern; confidentiality is important but straightforwardly addressed through anonymisation. For a study of underage gang members using covert observation, harm (to participants and researcher), deception (violating informed consent), confidentiality (disclosures of criminal activity) and access (via gatekeepers or snowball sampling) are all live and interconnected problems that require specific, reasoned responses. The mark scheme rewards practical reasoning in context, not a generic list.

Key Fact

Ethical issues in sociological research are not abstract principles but practical problems with practical solutions. Informed consent → written consent form + right to withdraw. Confidentiality → anonymisation + secure data storage. Harm → debrief + support signposting + ethics committee approval. Covert research violates informed consent but may be justified where the study could not be done otherwise and the social value is high.
exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark Identify and Describe question on ethical issues, identify a specific issue (not just “ethics”) and describe both what the problem is and how a researcher would address it. The common error is to describe the problem at length without proposing a practical solution. For a 12-mark Discuss on whether ethical constraints make certain research impossible or inadvisable, structure your argument around specific methods and contexts: e.g. covert participant observation of a criminal network is ethically problematic (deception violates informed consent, researcher safety) but may be the only method that produces valid data. A Mastering answer weighs the ethical cost against the research benefit and reaches a clear judgement, rather than simply listing both sides in parallel. Never treat the three ethical principles as a checklist — always apply them to the specific research scenario in the question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Practical constraints on research are time (affects method choice), cost (limits scale) and access (gatekeepers control entry to populations; hard-to-reach groups require alternative sampling strategies such as snowball sampling).
  • Three ethical principles: informed consent (voluntary agreement after full information), confidentiality (protecting identifying information) and harm to participants (minimising psychological, physical and reputational risk). Each has practical solutions: consent forms, anonymisation, debrief sessions, ethics committee approval.
  • Ethics are not a checklist — they must be applied to the specific research context. Covert observation violates informed consent but may be justified for hard-to-access populations where the social benefit is high. The tension between research goals and ethical obligations is a real and ongoing feature of sociological practice.

practice_questions.text:
Which term describes individuals or organisations who control access to a research population and whose permission must be obtained before research begins?
A) Respondents
B) Gatekeepers
C) Sampling frames
D) Pilot participants
Define the term 'informed consent' as used in sociological research ethics.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating consent requires participants to agree to take part; 1 mark for indicating they must be given full, honest information about the study and must agree voluntarily, with the right to withdraw. Example: 'Informed consent means that research participants must be given clear and honest information about the study, including its purpose and how their data will be used, and must voluntarily agree to take part before data collection begins.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one practical issue that sociologists face when conducting research and describe how it can affect the quality of the data collected.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a practical issue (time, cost or access). Up to 2 marks for describing how it affects data quality. Example: identifying access (1 mark) and describing that if a gatekeeper (such as a school head teacher) restricts access to certain participants — for example, excluding students with poor behaviour records from a study of school exclusion — the resulting sample will be biased and unrepresentative, meaning the findings cannot be generalised and the validity of the research is undermined (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two ethical issues that a sociologist might face when conducting research with vulnerable participants, and explain how each can be addressed.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for the first ethical issue: e.g. harm to participants — discussing traumatic experiences (abuse, bereavement) may cause psychological distress; the researcher can address this by offering a debrief session after the interview, providing signposting to relevant support services, and having a clear protocol for stopping if the participant shows signs of distress (1 mark for identifying harm, 1 mark for an appropriate solution). Up to 2 marks for the second ethical issue: e.g. informed consent with children — children cannot legally give consent themselves; the researcher must obtain written consent from a parent or guardian as well as assent from the child, and must explain the research in age-appropriate language (1 mark for identifying the consent problem, 1 mark for the practical solution).

practice_questions.text: Identify one ethical problem created by using covert observation as a research method and describe how a researcher might attempt to address it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an ethical problem specific to covert observation (e.g. deception violates informed consent; participants cannot withdraw because they do not know they are being studied; the researcher may observe illegal activity and face a legal or moral dilemma). Up to 2 marks for describing how it might be addressed. Example: identifying that covert observation involves deception, violating informed consent (1 mark) and explaining that some researchers address this by conducting a debrief as soon as the covert phase is complete — informing participants of the research, offering them the right to withdraw their data, and seeking retrospective consent — though critics argue this does not fully resolve the original deception (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: "Ethical guidelines make some of the most valuable sociological research impossible to conduct." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour: some research questions (studying gang violence, covert institutional racism, hidden drug networks) genuinely cannot be investigated ethically through fully consented, transparent methods; the Hawthorne effect means fully transparent research produces less valid data on sensitive behaviour; historical sociological research that violated consent (covert observation of private behaviour) produced findings that shaped policy. Arguments against: ethical guidelines protect vulnerable participants from exploitation; the BSA guidelines provide practical solutions (anonymisation, debriefs, ethics committees) that allow sensitive research to proceed; research that violates ethical principles is rejected by academic journals and ethics committees, and the findings lack credibility; feminist researchers argue participant-centred approaches produce richer and more valid data than covert extraction. At least two perspectives and named methods/examples cited. A clear supported judgement about where the balance lies.

Secure: Both sides addressed. At least one named method or context. A judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive. Some relevant points. Conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of ethical issues. Little evaluative engagement. No clear judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which ethical principle requires that participants be given full, honest information about a study and must voluntarily agree to take part?
An organisation (such as a school or prison) that controls access to a research population is called a:
The ethical principle that personal information about participants must be kept private and not used to identify individuals is called '______'.
The three practical issues sociologists face in research are time, cost and '______'.
Match each ethical issue to its appropriate practical solution.

pairs.definition: Provide a written consent form explaining the study and include the right to withdraw at any time
Anonymise all names and locations in published findings and store data securely
Offer a debrief session and signpost to support services after discussing sensitive topics
Debrief participants as soon as possible and offer retrospective withdrawal of data

flashcard_questions.a: Participants must receive full, honest information about the study and voluntarily agree to take part before it begins.
Personal information provided by participants must be protected and not used to identify them in publications.
Any psychological, physical or reputational risk the research process poses to the people being studied.
An individual or organisation that controls access to a research population and must grant permission for the study.

flashcard_questions.q: How can informed consent be obtained from children?
flashcard_questions.a: Written consent from a parent or guardian, plus age-appropriate assent from the child themselves.

flashcard_questions.q: How does covert observation violate ethical principles?
flashcard_questions.a: It involves deception: participants do not know they are being studied, so cannot give informed consent or withdraw.

flashcard_questions.q: What practical solution addresses harm after a sensitive interview?
flashcard_questions.a: A debrief session with signposting to relevant support services.
When people alter their behaviour because they know they are being observed or studied.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is time a significant practical issue in sociological research?
flashcard_questions.a: Longitudinal studies or ethnographic fieldwork can take years, limiting what most researchers can realistically undertake.
Replacing participants' real names and locations with codes or pseudonyms in published findings and data files.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is access a significant practical issue when studying hard-to-reach populations?
flashcard_questions.a: Gatekeepers may restrict entry and snowball sampling may produce biased, unrepresentative samples.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the professional body whose ethical guidelines UK sociologists follow.

glossary_terms.definition: The ethical principle that participants must receive full, honest information about a study and must voluntarily agree to take part before data collection begins.
The ethical principle that personal information provided by research participants must be kept private and not used to identify individuals.
Any psychological, physical, reputational or legal risk that the research process poses to the people being studied.
An individual or organisation that controls access to a research population and whose permission must be obtained before the research can proceed.
A population that is difficult for researchers to identify or contact, such as undocumented migrants or members of criminal networks.
A post-research session in which participants are told the full purpose of the study and offered support if sensitive topics were discussed.
Deliberately misleading research participants about the nature or purpose of a study; used in covert research and generally in violation of informed consent principles.

hero_image_caption: Ethical research protects participants while pursuing knowledge that benefits society.
